notable_claims: The University of Waterloo implemented a ban on certain newsgroups.
Computer scientists and librarians were absent from the committee that decided which content was banned.
classification.summary: Electronic Frontier Canada expressed concern over a newsgroup ban implemented at the University of Waterloo. The organization argued that the ban constituted 'prior restraint' on the rights of faculty, students, and staff. They specifically noted a lack of computer scientists and librarians on the decision-making committee.
classification.title: Electronic Frontier Canada press release

notable_claims: The University of Waterloo previously banned the 'rec.humor.funny' newsgroup in 1988 and several sex-related groups before reversing those decisions in 1991.
No Canadian court had decided that any message on any Usenet newsgroup was illegal as of February 1994.
The committee deciding on computer content lacked representation from computer scientists and librarians.
classification.summary: Electronic Frontier Canada (EFC) issued a press release condemning the University of Waterloo for censoring five Usenet newsgroups. The EFC argues that this censorship constitutes 'prior restraint' and sets a dangerous precedent regarding free speech in academic computing environments. The group highlights a double standard where controversial materials are permitted in physical libraries but banned on electronic networks.
classification.title: Electronic Frontier Canada press release

notable_claims: University staff running online archives should clearly distinguish whether the archive is an official university resource or a private one.
classification.summary: A forwarded post discussing the distinction between university-sponsored and private online archives hosted by staff members. The author argues that clear boundaries must be established to avoid confusion regarding institutional responsibility for such content.
classification.title: Re: Fanny Hill Rides Again!

identity.subject: Re: Fanny Hill Rides Again! (was Re: Censor on Internet..Pt-1)

notable_claims: If a university digital archive is treated as a library, its selection policy should align with the Library Bill of Rights.
Individuals operating university resources may be viewed as state agents if they lack clear personal editorial authority.
The legal status of whether a digital archive constitutes a limited public forum or nonpublic forum was unclear at the time.
classification.summary: Carl Kadie discusses the legal complexities of censorship within university-hosted digital archives, specifically regarding whether such archives function as public forums or personal editorial property. He examines how the First and Fourteenth Amendments apply to individuals acting as state agents versus private volunteers on campus networks. The discussion uses the removal of 'Fanny Hill' as a case study for comparing digital archives to physical libraries and student newspapers.
classification.title: Re: Fanny Hill Rides Again! (was Re: Censor on Internet..Pt-1)

identity.subject: Re: Fanny Hill Rides Again! (was Re: Censor on Internet..Pt-1)

notable_claims: The University of Guelph scanned all incoming private mail for specific keywords related to a legal ban.
Users responded to this surveillance by seeking tools to scramble their mail.
classification.summary: A report claims that the University of Guelph began scanning all incoming email, including private messages, for references to Paul Bernardo and Karla Homolka. This surveillance was allegedly intended to prevent violations of a legal ban on publishing details about the case. In response, some users sought methods to encrypt or scramble their communications.

notable_claims: The university's curation of newsgroup content for local users may be legally viewed as publication, unlike the acquisition of print media.
classification.summary: A legal advisor at McGill University argued that the university's handling of newsgroup data differed legally from its acquisition of print newspapers. The advisor claimed that packaging a newsgroup for local users constitutes processing and editing, which could be construed as publication.
classification.title: McGill U. treating computer media differently than paper media

identity.subject: McGill U. treating computer media differently than paper media

notable_claims: The university legal advisor claimed that packaging a newsgroup for local users constitutes 'processing, editing and promulgating,' which could be construed as publication.
The administration argued that allowing local access while blocking external propagation would constitute 'inter institutional censorship' and 'institutional peeping Tomism.'
classification.summary: Correspondence between a faculty member and McGill University's legal advisor reveals a policy where 'banned material' was permitted in print form in libraries but prohibited on campus electronic networks. The university argued that providing access to Usenet newsgroups constituted 'publication' due to the technical process of processing and promulgating data, whereas possessing print media did not.
classification.title: McGill U. treating computer media differently than paper media

identity.subject: McGill U. treating computer media differently than paper media

classification.summary: A repost discussing a dispute with McGill University's Legal Advisor regarding the banning of digital materials. The author argues against the advisor's claim that banning material can be a means to prevent censorship.
classification.title: McGill U. treating computer media differently than paper media

identity.subject: Re: McGill U. treating computer media differently than paper media

notable_claims: The university legal advisor claimed that banning material is a way to prevent censorship rather than impose it.
Kadie argues that treating automatic Usenet processing as 'publishing' creates an illogical liability for the university regarding all information it processes.
classification.summary: Carl Kadie critiques a memorandum from McGill University's legal advisor regarding the banning of Usenet newsgroups. The university argued that providing access to newsgroups constituted 'publication,' whereas Kadie argues this is an automatic process akin to library cataloging and that blocking access constitutes censorship.
classification.title: Re: McGill U. treating computer media differently than paper media
